query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single‐phase high-entropy alloy, deformation at intermediate temperatures promotes rapid, dislocation‐assisted migration of the principal elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, and Mn in fcc HEAs) to grain boundaries, creating local compositional inhomogeneities that reduce interface cohesion and trigger brittle intergranular cracking. By contrast, if preexisting nanoscale precipitates (engineered via a controlled heat treatment or minor compositional adjustment) are introduced to act as sinks for these embrittling elements, the concentration of the segregants at the GBs is reduced and toughness is retained.
generation.material_initial_state: A compositionally complex, single-phase HEA (for example, a CrMnFeCoNi-type alloy) with homogeneous element distribution and no preexisting intermetallic phases.
generation.intervention: Subject part of the alloy to a tailored thermal treatment or slight compositional adjustment that induces the controlled formation of nanoscale, Cr-rich precipitates along grain boundaries, while keeping the overall single-phase character intact.
generation.conditions: Testing under intermediate temperatures (approximately 500–700 °C) and moderate strain rates that are active enough to drive dislocation motion and diffusion but below melting/oxidation thresholds, simulating demanding engineering service environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that, in the untreated state, accumulate segregated principal elements leading to decohesion versus grain boundaries that are modified by preexisting nanoscale precipitates which sequester embrittling species.
generation.mechanism: Under service-like thermal and mechanical conditions, the high lattice distortion and dislocation activity in HEAs drives fast migration of principal elemental species to the GBs, locally depleting the matrix and inducing brittle intergranular fracture. In samples with engineered nano-precipitates at GBs, these precipitates preferentially absorb the migrating elements, thereby mitigating detrimental segregation and preserving high cohesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline single-phase HEA that exhibits marked intergranular cracking and reduced toughness, the treated alloy with preformed grain boundary precipitates will display improved ductility and a shift from predominantly intergranular to more transgranular fracture modes, indicating enhanced toughness.
generation.baseline: The initial single-phase HEA without engineered grain boundary modification, which under intermediate temperature tensile loading shows fast segregation of principal elements to GBs and brittle, intergranular fracture behavior.
generation.boundary: This effect is predicted under intermediate temperature loading conditions (approximately 500–700 °C) and strain rates that activate dislocation-assisted atomic diffusion; the mechanism may not govern behavior at cryogenic temperatures or temperatures so high that other degradation mechanisms (e.g., oxidation or complete intermetallic formation) dominate.
generation.uncertainty: While evidence from studies such as PMC6897545 (showing segregation-induced ductility loss) and PMC11407990 (demonstrating deformation-induced segregation dynamics) supports the segregation mechanism in HEAs, quantitative thresholds for segregation levels and the optimal precipitate volume fraction remain to be established. It is uncertain how broadly this mechanism applies across different HEA systems without further systematic studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of otherwise identical single-phase HEA samples. One set remains in the as-cast single-phase state. The other set is subjected to a controlled thermal treatment (or minor alloying addition) designed to induce the formation of nanoscale, Cr-rich precipitates along GBs. Perform tensile tests at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 650 °C) at controlled strain rates. Characterize the grain boundary chemistry before and after deformation using atom probe tomography or TEM-EDS, and analyze the fracture surfaces to distinguish intergranular versus transgranular failure modes.
measurements: Fractography to identify intergranular versus transgranular fracture
Grain boundary composition and precipitate distribution via APT/TEM-EDS
Comparison of crack initiation sites and propagation paths
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated HEA with engineered grain boundary precipitates does not show a statistically significant improvement in toughness (e.g., increased ductility and reduced intergranular fracture) relative to the untreated baseline, OR if both sample sets exhibit similar levels of principal element segregation at grain boundaries despite the intervention, then the hypothesis that dynamic segregation is the primary mechanism for toughness degradation in these HEAs is falsified.
